title: Genesis 39:1–18
context: Joseph is sold into Potiphar’s house. The LORD is with him; blessing spills onto an Egyptian household. Potiphar’s wife presses him day after day; he refuses as sin against God, flees, and is framed by the garment he left behind.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Historic words on the LORD with Joseph, and refusing Potiphar’s wife—so each camp speaks in its own voice beside Genesis 39:1–18.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: How can I sin against God—Not only how shall I do it and sin against my master, my mistress, myself, my own body and soul, but against God? - Gracious souls look upon this as the worst thing in sin, that it is against God, against his nature and his dominion, against his love and his design. They that love God, for this reason hate sin.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 39:9)

reformed.quote: Here that which has been lately alluded to more clearly appears, that the grace of God shone forth in Joseph, in no common or usual manner; since it became thus manifest to a man who was a heathen, and, in this respect, blind. How much more base is our ingratitude, if we do not refer all our prosperous events to God as their author; seeing that Scripture often teaches us, that nothing proceeding from men, whether counsels, or labors, or any means which they can devise, will profit them, except so far as God gives his blessing.

verses.text: Now Joseph had been brought down to Egypt, and Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard, an Egyptian, had bought him from the Ishmaelites who had brought him down there.
verses.arminianNotes: Brought down, bought, named owners. The narrator does not flinch at slavery’s facts. Classical Arminians still see a man, not a pawn: Joseph will soon have to choose under this roof.
verses.reformedNotes: The Ishmaelites of chapter 37 deliver him to Potiphar, captain of the guard. Reformed readers hear providence in the “down”: this house sits on the road to prison and, later, to famine-saving power.

verses.text: The LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man, and he was in the house of his Egyptian master.
verses.arminianNotes: Presence first, then success. Arminian reading: the LORD’s nearness does not erase Joseph’s work in the house; it enables a faithful walk in a pagan master’s rooms.
verses.reformedNotes: The chapter’s thesis: “the LORD was with Joseph.” Reformed accent: success is explained before it is seen. Location in an Egyptian house is not absence of God; it is God with him there.

verses.text: His master saw that the LORD was with him and that the LORD caused all that he did to succeed in his hands.
verses.arminianNotes: Even Potiphar can see whose hand makes the work flourish. Arminians hear a witness to outsiders: faithful labor under God is meant to be visible, not hidden piety.
verses.reformedNotes: The LORD caused the success; the master merely saw it. Reformed confession: common-grace eyes can notice fruit God produces. The cause is named twice: the LORD was with him, and the LORD caused it.

verses.text: So Joseph found favor in his sight and attended him, and he made him overseer of his house and put him in charge of all that he had.
verses.arminianNotes: Favor, attendance, charge of all. Trust is given; it can still be betrayed. Arminian pastoral: stewardship is a real responsibility. Joseph will soon refuse to use this trust as a bed.
verses.reformedNotes: Favor in Potiphar’s sight follows the LORD’s presence, not charm alone. Reformed note: overseer of all is providence loading Joseph with a test equal to the trust.

verses.text: From the time that he made him overseer in his house and over all that he had, the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake; the blessing of the LORD was on all that he had, in house and field.
verses.arminianNotes: An Egyptian house is blessed for Joseph’s sake—Abraham’s “you will be a blessing” already leaking into Egypt. Arminians gladly trace mercy beyond Israel’s line; outsiders taste the LORD’s kindness through a faithful servant.
verses.reformedNotes: Blessing on house and field is the Abrahamic promise in miniature. Reformed accent: “for Joseph’s sake” is covenantal, not luck. God prospers a pagan household because He is with the man He sent there.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear Abraham’s blessing reaching Egypt. Arminians typically stress sincere kindness that spills to the nations through a willing servant; Reformed readers typically stress that the LORD sovereignly blesses for Joseph’s sake as He advances the covenant.

verses.text: So he left all that he had in Joseph’s charge, and because of him he had no concern about anything but the food he ate. Now Joseph was handsome in form and appearance.
verses.arminianNotes: Total trust, then the narrator’s warning: Joseph is handsome. Gift and vulnerability sit in one verse. Arminian reading prepares a real temptation that must be refused, not a script Joseph cannot help.
verses.reformedNotes: Potiphar’s ease and Joseph’s appearance are both under the author’s lamp. Reformed readers do not treat beauty as fate. The LORD who blesses the house will also keep the man when desire turns predatory.

verses.text: And after a time his master’s wife cast her eyes on Joseph and said, “Lie with me.”
verses.arminianNotes: Desire looks, then commands. The sin is named without perfume. Classical Arminians insist Joseph can refuse: the command is not his destiny.
verses.reformedNotes: “After a time” marks a test after prosperity. Reformed note: the demand is blunt because wickedness often is. What follows will show whether “the LORD was with him” includes holy fear.

verses.text: But he refused and said to his master’s wife, “Behold, because of me my master has no concern about anything in the house, and he has put everything that he has in my charge.
verses.arminianNotes: He refused—first word. Then he reasons from trust: my master has no concern because of me. Arminian pastoral: saying no is a grace-enabled act. Loyalty to a human master is already a reason to stop.
verses.reformedNotes: Refusal is the fruit of the LORD’s presence, not a solo moral stunt. Reformed accent: Joseph names the trust he has been given. Integrity here is stewardship under God, spoken out loud.

verses.text: He is not greater in this house than I am, nor has he kept back anything from me except you, because you are his wife. How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?”
verses.arminianNotes: The climax is Godward: great wickedness, sin against God. Marriage is named; so is the LORD. Arminians hear a conscience that can still say no. Adultery is not a private slip; it is sin against God, freely refused.
verses.reformedNotes: Joseph’s theology of sex is vertical. Reformed confession: the decisive argument is not career risk but God. Presence in Potiphar’s house includes the God who sees in secret. The refusal is real; its root is fear of the LORD.
verses.keyContrast: Both prize the refusal as sin-against-God. Arminians typically stress Joseph’s responsible, grace-enabled no; Reformed readers typically stress that the LORD’s presence produces this holy fear, not mere willpower.

verses.text: And as she spoke to Joseph day after day, he would not listen to her, to lie beside her or to be with her.
verses.arminianNotes: Day after day: temptation repeats. He would not listen—ongoing refusal, not a single heroic hour. Arminian application: perseverance in the small nos, including avoiding even “being with her.”
verses.reformedNotes: Sustained pressure, sustained resistance. Reformed comfort: the God who is with Joseph keeps him through repetition. Distance (“not… with her”) is wisdom, not priggishness.

verses.text: But one day, when he went into the house to do his work and none of the men of the house was there in the house,
verses.arminianNotes: Ordinary work, empty house. Opportunity is not permission. Arminians refuse the excuse that circumstance made the sin inevitable; Joseph still has to choose in the quiet.
verses.reformedNotes: Providence includes this empty house. Reformed reading: the test is arranged in time, yet the LORD remains with him. Isolation will prove the fear of God or the lack of it.

verses.text: she caught him by his garment, saying, “Lie with me.” But he left his garment in her hand and fled and got out of the house.
verses.arminianNotes: Caught, commanded, fled. Leaving the garment is costly and right. Arminian pastoral: sometimes holiness looks like running. Fleeing is not cowardice; it is obedience when words have already been spent.
verses.reformedNotes: Flight is the appointed means. Reformed note: Joseph’s feet preach what his mouth already said. The LORD with him does not make him statue-still; it sends him out of the house.

verses.text: And as soon as she saw that he had left his garment in her hand and had fled out of the house,
verses.arminianNotes: She sees the garment and the flight. Evidence of his refusal becomes her prop. Arminian warning: scorned desire can turn to lying in a breath.
verses.reformedNotes: The narrator slows the turn from assault to plot. Reformed readers watch providence leave a garment in her hand—the very token that will send Joseph toward the prison God will use.

verses.text: she called to the men of her household and said to them, “See, he has brought among us a Hebrew to laugh at us. He came in to me to lie with me, and I cried out with a loud voice.
verses.arminianNotes: She reverses the story and racializes it: “a Hebrew to laugh at us.” False witness plus contempt. Arminians name both as sin. Joseph’s ethnicity is weaponized; the household is invited to hate.
verses.reformedNotes: Slander recruits the staff. Reformed accent: “he has brought among us” blames Potiphar too. God is still with the Hebrew she mocks; her loud voice does not rewrite what happened.

verses.text: And as soon as he heard that I lifted up my voice and cried out, he left his garment beside me and fled and got out of the house.”
verses.arminianNotes: She rearranges the garment: “beside me,” not torn away as he fled. Lying is careful. Arminian reading: words can invert holiness into guilt. Truth still exists even when the room believes her.
verses.reformedNotes: The lie is almost the truth, re-aimed. Reformed note: God hears the real cry Joseph never made. The garment will travel to Potiphar; so will this fiction.

verses.text: Then she laid up his garment by her until his master came home,
verses.arminianNotes: She stores the prop. Delay is part of the trap. Arminian pastoral: sin often waits for an audience. Joseph cannot retrieve his name from a folded cloak.
verses.reformedNotes: The garment waits like a loaded witness. Reformed readers see the master’s coming as the next hinge of providence—toward prison, not toward clearing.

verses.text: and she told him the same story, saying, “The Hebrew servant, whom you have brought among us, came in to me to laugh at me.
verses.arminianNotes: Same story, aimed at the husband: your Hebrew, your fault. Arminians hear the cruelty of pinning assault on the innocent and on the man who trusted him.
verses.reformedNotes: “Whom you have brought” spreads the blame. Reformed accent: the LORD brought Joseph to Egypt; she credits Potiphar. Two accounts of agency now compete; only one is true.

verses.text: But as soon as I lifted up my voice and cried, he left his garment beside me and fled out of the house.”
verses.arminianNotes: The speech ends where verse 15 ended. Repetition hardens the lie. Arminian warning: a story told twice is still false. Joseph’s next hearing will be a prison door, not a fair trial.
verses.reformedNotes: The lie is complete. Reformed comfort is not in Potiphar’s justice but in the refrain still to come: the LORD was with Joseph—even after this sentence.
